Tonight's starting five is inside every number from the moment lineups post. A reserve who starts gets his extra minutes, and a usual starter left out of the five is cut and flagged. On 1,199 of last season's games that the lessons never saw, minutes at tip-off landed 19% closer and points 4% closer than the app as it was.

New context: how crowded tonight's rotation is. When several players are out, or everyone is back, minutes are not shared out evenly: the regular bench keeps most of its minutes on a crowded night and picks up less than an even split on a short-handed one. Learned from finished games, this alone brought minutes 4% closer at tip-off and 6% closer before lineups post (same 1,199 games).
The first quarter was the app's blind spot. Six to nine minutes in, minutes now land 10 to 14% closer and points 2 to 3% closer (same 1,199 games).
Between checkpoints the app blends the lessons of the two nearest stages instead of jumping from one to the next. At 15 minutes in, minutes landed 8% closer and points 1% closer (400 unseen games).
About one player a game who went on to play 10+ minutes had no number at tip-off: deep-bench players on short-handed nights and players back from a layoff. They now get one as soon as lineups post.

Before tip-off each player's number answers 'what if he plays', because a pick on a player who sits is no action. The game score is scaled to the minutes a team can really play. Final score at tip-off: 6.6% closer on those 1,199 games.
The test got stricter too: each past game is replayed with exactly the list the phone sees at tip-off (players already ruled out are not on it), for the old app and the new one alike.
From halftime on the gain is small (0.3% on points at halftime), and in the last six minutes nothing moved: by then the game itself tells most of the story.
The lessons built into the app come from 3,709 games across four seasons: every final through Nov 9 (1,314 before). Every plus edge shown is saved and graded on this phone: see EDGE RECORD above.
